title: Multi-tenant virtualized GPU scenario matrix and cost/latency notes
summary: Working draft exploring latency vs cost tradeoffs for multi-tenant GPU virtualization strategies (MIG split, NVIDIA vGPU, and single-tenant instances). Intended as internal collateral for product and infra planning — focuses on p50/p95 observed across synthetic conversational workloads and token-normalized cost estimates.
background: We frequently get asks from product and customers: can we offer cheaper reservations using GPU multiplexing without killing tail latency? This doc aggregates a small-batch of targeted experiments run on our staging cluster to surface practical tradeoffs and an actionable scenario matrix for Dedicated and Private offerings.
goals: 1) Compare latency distribution (p50/p95/p99) and cost-per-1M-tokens for three virtualization modes. 2) Identify sweet spots for mixed-tenancy packing with acceptable tail latency. 3) Produce simple guidance for pricing and autoscaler rules.
methodology: Workload: conversational turns (avg 120 tokens/request, seq len 512 max) using an Llama-like 13B model profile compiled with our runtime. Traffic shapes: steady 100 rps, burst 300 rps (10s windows), and sessionized traffic (concurrent sessions=120). Metrics: p50/p95/p99 token latency, CPU/GPU utilization, effective throughput, and normalized cost estimate (cloud GPU cost mapped to per-token). Each experiment ran for 30 minutes after warmup. Quantization levels tested: FP16 baseline, dynamic INT8 (post-training quant), and mixed precision with KV-cache enabled.
test_configs: A) Single-tenant A100-80GB dedicated (one container per GPU). B) MIG 7g.30gb slices (4-way split on A100 equivalent). C) NVIDIA vGPU-style time-slice (simulated with container multiplexing and our scheduler). D) Small-GPU fleet (T4-like) as cost baseline. All runs used identical model weights and the same batching policy: opportunistic batching with 10ms max wait.
note_on_validity: Small-n experiments on staging hardware — absolute numbers will change on prod hardware. Interpret relative deltas, not absolute ms. We did not account for cross-tenant noisy neighbors beyond synthetic co-tenancy patterns; real tenant interference could worsen p99.
results_overview: High level: MIG gives best cost-per-token for steady moderate throughput but has a measurable p95 uplift (~15-30%) versus single-tenant. vGPU/time-slice gives lowest peak cost but has the worst p99 tails under short bursts. Quantization to INT8 reduced per-token cost by ~28% and reduced p50 slightly, but increases p95 for time-sliced modes unless KV cache hit rate > 70%.

observations:
- MIG (4-way) strikes a practical compromise: ~35% cheaper than single-tenant with modest p95 degradation. Good for background/low-priority tenants.
- vGPU/time-slice can unlock much cheaper list price but causes high p99s on short bursts and sessionized patterns; not recommended for interactive SLAs.
- INT8 is attractive on cost but needs careful evals for hallucination/regression; also interacts with batching: smaller batches amplify quantization jitter on tails.
- KV-cache hit rate is a first-order moderator: with h>70% tail differences shrink dramatically because most requests short-circuit the model.
- Autoscaler policies that allow transient burst capacity (short-lived dedicated slot warmups) mitigate vGPU tail pain at the cost of higher average spend.
sessionized_breakdown: Session test (120 concurrent sessions, random turn intervals): MIG p95 increased 1.3x relative to steady; vGPU p95 increased 1.8x. Tail (p99) amplified more: MIG ~1.6x, vGPU ~2.3x. Conclusion: multi-tenant packing is riskier for sessionized interactive workloads.
recommended_scenarios_matrix: Simple guidance for product/infra — row = customer profile, recommended mode, notes:
scenarios_matrix_rows: Consumer chat / high-interactivity -> single-tenant or dedicated MIG with SLA tier; avoid vGPU
Background batch generation -> vGPU-sim or small-GPU fleet, prioritize cost
SaaS mixed workloads -> MIG for non-critical tenants, single-tenant for premium tenants
Burst-heavy but tolerant-latency -> vGPU + burst reserver policy (short dedicated buffers)

conclusions: For Dedicated product packaging: offer three explicit capacity modes (single-tenant, MIG-economy, vGPU-spot) with clear latency expectations. Invest in autoscaling primitives and KV-cache guidance — these materially change the delta between modes. Larger experiments needed before GA pricing changes.
